Agent.text: I'll start with the overview of what was captured.
The app ships its presets as real data files, so I'm reading those next, along with how they're organised and what the app says about them.
I'm listing the image catalogue, preset names and the app's wording next, since those show how the preset screen is laid out.
Next I'm opening the main program. I want the code that lays out the preset picker, not just the wording around it.
The preset screen's own code is around `0x1005966d4`–`0x10059f400`, so I'm reading those functions for tile sizes, grouping and how the preview thumbnails get made.
The image catalogue has plain JPEGs, so I can pull some into a temp folder and see what the app's screens look like. They're for reference only and won't go into your app.
The preset look depends on one decision only you can make, so I'm asking you now while I keep reading the code.
`0x10059adac` is the one strip inside the preset code, so the presets sit in a horizontal row. I'm reading that function now.
The range scan points to `0x1005548c8`, which holds ±3000 and ±100, and `0x100553f6c`, which holds 6500. Those look like the Temperature and Tint controls, so I'm reading them next.
The code confirms Temperature runs ±3000 around 6500K and Tint runs ±100. Two checks remain before I build: how tall the preset strip is in the editor, and the exact interface colours.
The shader files list the steps, such as exposure, contrast and colour grade, but not the order they run in. I'm logging that as an open question and setting up the project.
The project is set up. Before writing the interface I'm checking how this version of the window library works.
The library files hadn't finished downloading, so I'm fetching them and then checking the interfaces.
I've finished studying the original and I'm now writing the app: the colour engine, my own presets, then the interface.
The colour engine is written. Next are my own presets, the sample picture, and saving.
Next is the interface: drawn icons, preset tiles built from the sizes in the code, sliders, and the photo view.
One build error is left, in how dropped files are read. I'm checking the library's new interface for that.
It builds and the screenshot option works, so I'm looking at the picture it produced.

Agent.text: The strip's 20-point bottom space checks out. Next I'll trace the colour pipeline through its filter types and find where the panel sets the strip's height.
A 4,309-line function that reads the colour tables looks very much like the master render. It's too big to return in one piece, so I'll pull the saved copy and go through it.
The export has the full function. I'll pull it out and list which fields it uses, in order, since that sequence is the order the colour steps run.
I'm adding a short progress list here, since the rest of this work splits into clear steps. Then I'll trace the order of the steps through the render function.
I'll set up the progress list, then finish mapping the render function: the rest of its sequence, plus a table of field names against their offsets from the class's own records.
Now I have all the names and offsets. I'll label the render function with them and read off the actual sequence.
That failure is only a path mismatch: Windows Python can't read Git Bash's `/tmp` path. I'll switch the script to relative paths and run it from that folder.
The batch tool uses the built-in engine, which stopped short of this region. The single-function tool goes through Ghidra, so I'll call that for each one.

Agent.text: All checks pass. The one question left needs the original running on a real iPhone, which I can't do from here. I'll note in that record what I did instead and close out the list.

You now have a working desktop version of the photo editor with the original's preset strip: square tiles showing your own photo with each look applied, white caption bars that turn blue when selected, and thin lines between groups. It also has the sliders, film and effects tools, masks, crop, colour tables, saving your own presets and export, and it passes every Craft Anything check.

In this last round I read the original's code and fixed two things. The preset panel now uses the original's real sizing rule, 20% of the window height, and the colour steps run in the original's order, with colour tables after the sliders, which changes how every look comes out.

The preset names and colour tables are my own recreations, not the originals, so the looks are similar in style but won't match exactly, and the slider strengths are my estimates. Some of the original's rarer tools, such as Super 8 and tone curves, aren't included. I also never saw the original running, because no picture of that screen exists in its files, so the panel is built from the code's measurements and hasn't been compared with the real thing.

If you can, send a phone screenshot of the original's preset screen and ask me to match anything that looks different.
